#5342. Bitcoin ETF Loses $570M: More Than Half of BTC Supply Falls Out of Profit

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin sell-off is starting to hurt investors who bought well before the price crash. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $569.7 million yesterday, while on-chain data showed only 47.3% of BTC supply remaining in profit.

BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for $509.3 million of Monday’s withdrawals, dwarfing flows across the rest of the ETF market. Fidelity’s FBTC bucked the trend with $13.3 million in inflows, but that was nowhere near enough to offset the selling.

Bitcoin has struggled to turn its latest price rebound into a lasting recovery. Buyers briefly pushed BTC above $64,000, but then reversed the gain, sending Bitcoin back below $60,000.

BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for $509.3 million of Monday’s $569.7 million Bitcoin ETF outflow. The fund’s withdrawals alone contributed almost 90% of the day’s total, making it the biggest driver of the sell-off.

Fidelity’s FBTC was the lone fund to post an inflow, attracting $13.3 million. The remaining products either recorded no flows or saw smaller withdrawals, leaving IBIT firmly at the center of Monday’s exodus.

Glassnode’s supply-in-profit metric fell to 46%, down from 54.2% one week earlier. The shift means most circulating Bitcoin is now held outside the profit category, marking a sharp deterioration in market profitability.

The change is big and maybe bad at the same time because it alters how investors may react to another drop. Holders who were comfortably sitting on gains can wait out volatility. Those who have watched their positions turn red may instead use the next rebound to reduce exposure.

Short-term holders are facing difficult conditions, with net unrealized profit and loss reportedly dropping to negative 18.3% as pressure mounts on coins acquired more recently. Realized losses have also climbed as investors sell below their acquisition prices.

It does leave the market more vulnerable to disappointment. A weak rebound could convince some holders that waiting for a full recovery is no longer worth the risk.

Bitcoin Hyper is heading into its final two days before launch, and the presale is still offering $HYPER at just $0.0136. With more than $33.2 million raised and staking rewards of 35% APY, the project is attracting attention before its November 26 token launch.

The timing is what makes this interesting. Buyers are entering before named centralized exchange listings are disclosed and before broader market exposure could put Bitcoin Hyper in front of a much larger audience. At just 1.37 cents per token, $HYPER remains priced at its presale stage, with launch day rapidly approaching.

Bitcoin Hyper is also pitching more than another speculative token. Its Layer 2 aims to connect Bitcoin with Solana’s high-speed SVM execution environment, opening the door to faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications. BTC could move beyond simply holding value and become usable across a wider ecosystem.

The project is trying to bring Bitcoin liquidity into a new infrastructure layer. With the countdown nearly finished, the window to enter at presale pricing is getting increasingly tight.

The Bitcoin price needs to reclaim the $62,000–$66,000 area to give the recovery some credibility. That zone could present a difficult hurdle after the recent breakdown, particularly if ETF demand remains weak.

A sustained move above the range would put $74,100 back on the radar, near the reported average cost basis for short-term holders. Reaching that level would offer recent buyers an opportunity to exit closer to breakeven, and could create fresh selling pressure.

On the downside, losing $58,500 would leave June’s low exposed. A deeper decline could bring Bitcoin’s realized price at $53,700 into focus, a level that could become important if losses continue spreading.

Bitcoin price needs fresh demand to turn these battered positions into a recovery.

#5341. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

#5340. Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees and says he's in therapy

Huang admitted that he had failed employees, owned up to breaking Nvidia's code of conduct, and said he appreciated being given another opportunity

Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday and told them he is in therapy.

Huang called it "the hardest company meeting" he had held, according to Bloomberg. He admitted to employees that he had failed them, owned up to breaking Nvidia's code of conduct, and said he appreciated being given another opportunity to run the business he helped start.

Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned following revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The board said its vote was unanimous and followed a series of meetings with Huang and assurances from top U.S. officials that he did not post a national security risk. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress had served as interim CEO while keeping her CFO duties.

Huang credited the Trump administration with speedily sharing intelligence with Nvidia, which he said allowed the board to conclude that the dangers of bringing him back were small, according to The Wall Street Journal.

He said the board reached its decision after reviewing the evidence and getting assurance that national security was not at risk, and that the wishes of top government officials to have him back did not influence it, according to Bloomberg. Huang said President Donald Trump loves Nvidia. "He is my president," Huang said. "I am in service of making our president — our country — successful."

Huang focused on the code of conduct during the meeting. On Sunday, he told the board that there had been more affairs than the two widely reported in the media, according to The Journal. Those two involved an employee and an executive of a company that buys Nvidia's products, a person U.S. officials suspected of acting as an asset for Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia said a board committee of independent directors is investigating reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and that the inquiry will proceed to conclusion. Huang supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it, the company said.

Nvidia stock fell more than 7% in Tuesday trading after a rally on Monday.

#5339. Billionaire Frank Slootman gives 22,081 Montana kids $1,000 each for their Trump Accounts

Snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, are giving more than $22 million to children in their home state of Montana. The couple is putting $1,000 into the Trump Account of every Montana child born in 2023 or 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department announced on Nov. 19.

The gift covers 22,081 children, totaling $22,081,000. The Slootman Family Foundation said the money has already been deposited through the Treasury Department and invested in the children’s accounts, according to NBC Montana.

Those children were born too early for the federal government’s own $1,000 deposit, which goes only to children born from 2025 through 2028. The Slootmans’ gift gives them the same start. At $1,000 a child, it is also four times the per-child amount in Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion national pledge.

“Montana is the Last Best Place,” the Slootmans said in a statement. “We want to give Montana children an even faster start in life. The money in your account is yours, it cannot be accessed by anybody, not even by you until you are at least 18 years old. What you can do is watch it grow, ask for contributions on birthdays, holidays, and other special occasions to make your account compound in value even more.”

Gov. Greg Gianforte thanked the family for what he called “this significant investment.”

Frank Slootman, Snowflake’s chairman and former CEO, led the cloud data company through its 2020 initial public offering after taking two other technology companies, Data Domain and ServiceNow, public. Bloomberg Law reported that the Bloomberg Billionaires Index put his net worth at $3.1 billion when the gift was announced.

Slootman, born in the Netherlands, has lived in Bozeman for years. When Snowflake eliminated its corporate headquarters in 2021, it named its Bozeman office its principal executive office because Slootman and the company’s CFO lived in the city, Fortune reported at the time.

The family foundation has given to Montana causes before, including $1 million to American Prairie Foundation, a conservation group assembling a large prairie reserve in the state, in 2022 and $1.5 million in each of the next two years, according to its tax filings. This latest gift is on another scale: It roughly matches the $22.7 million in net assets the foundation reported at the end of 2024, the latest year for which its filings are public.

Slootman has also backed Montana Republicans. While he was ServiceNow’s CEO, he gave the maximum allowed contribution to Gianforte, then the state’s congressman, CNBC reported in 2021. Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican, publicly thanked the couple for the gift last week, calling it “an incredible bet on Montana’s future.”

Created under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax law, a Trump Account is a type of individual retirement account for children. Parents, relatives, and employers can contribute, generally up to a combined $5,000 a year during childhood. Contributions from charities to a broad group of children, such as every child born in a state in a given year, don’t count toward that cap.

The money goes into low-cost funds that track broad U.S. stock indexes, such as the S&P 500, so its value rises or falls with the market. Investment earnings generally aren’t taxed until you withdraw the money.

Families generally can’t withdraw the money until the calendar year the child turns 18. After that, traditional IRA rules apply, and withdrawals can trigger taxes and early withdrawal penalties.

The Treasury Department has opened accounts for eligible children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Nearly 70 million children now have one, a White House spokesman told Fortune this month. Only U.S. citizens born from Jan. 1, 2025, through Dec. 31, 2028, qualify for the government’s one-time $1,000 deposit.

Some Montana children covered by the Slootmans’ gift may have already received $250 from Michael and Susan Dell. The Dells’ gift reached 25 million children born from 2016 through 2024, starting in zip codes with the lowest median family incomes. The Slootmans’ announcement said 118,523 Montana children are eligible for the Dells’ $250.

A Montana child who qualified for both gifts would have $1,250 from the two couples.

Parents can claim their child’s account through the official Trump Accounts app by verifying their identity and their relationship to the child. Once an account is claimed, relatives can add their own contributions. Fortune has a guide to who gets the $1,000 and how to claim an account.

#5338. Wendy's is sued for allegedly coordinating menu prices across its franchise network

A proposed class action in Maryland also names NCR Voyix and seeks unspecified damages and an order halting the alleged pricing scheme

Wendy's $WEN and restaurant software provider NCR Voyix face a proposed class action in U.S. federal court in Maryland that accuses them of colluding to drive up what customers pay for menu items, allegedly by consolidating price-setting and pooling sales figures throughout Wendy's franchise system, according to Reuters.

Andy Garcia, a California resident, filed the suit on Monday, representing a group of Wendy's customers that numbers in the tens of thousands at minimum.

The complaint alleges that Wendy's pulls in and circulates register data on individual transactions via NCR Voyix's Aloha system. It says Wendy's relies on that data to align prices among outlets that ought to be rivals. The suit also alleges Wendy's obliges franchisees that compete against each other to run the Aloha software and hand over granular figures on their sales and prices.

Garcia alleges that Wendy's acts as a "common decisionmaker" across a network of thousands of independent franchisees plus the restaurants the company owns itself, controlling what consumers pay in breach of U.S. antitrust law. The lawsuit says the scheme dates to 2016 or earlier.

Allen Neumark, a lawyer for Garcia, said in a statement that Wendy's relies on a system for setting prices to rig the market for what it sells.

"Wendy's tells its investors that franchisees set their own prices. But this is false," Neumark said. "And when businesses that should be competing stop competing on price, consumers pay more."

The complaint asks for an unspecified amount in damages, along with a court order that would halt the alleged coordination of prices. Wendy's and NCR Voyix had not responded to requests for comment, according to Reuters.

The case follows a similar suit against McDonald's $MCD. That company has denied wrongdoing in a suit filed in October that accuses it of improperly using technology tools to fix prices, according to Reuters. The Wendy's case is one of a rising number of legal actions that question the way businesses use data and technology to set prices.

Wendy's is also dealing with falling sales. Franchisee Meritage Hospitality Group, which operates 314 Wendy's locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September. Same-store sales across Wendy's U.S. system had fallen for six consecutive quarters, down 7.8% in the first quarter of this year and 7.0% in the second.

#5337. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5336. After 40 investors rejected Jeff Bezos’ Amazon pitch, his parents offered $245,573 of their retirement savings

Sometimes the best investments are more about a gut feeling than hard numbers. At least that holds true for Jeff Bezos’ parents, who bet on their son when few others would.

In 1995, a mere two years before Amazon would go public, and more than 30 years  before it would surpass Walmart to clinch the No. 1 spot on the Fortune 500, Bezos received a lifeline from his parents.

According to a 1997 prospectus, his mother Jacklyn Gise Bezos, who died in 2025, and stepfather Miguel “Mike” Bezos, gave their son $245,573 from their savings so he could get his business off the ground. The six-figure sum represented a “large fraction” of their life savings at the time, according to Bezos, but it would eventually make them both billionaires.

Yet, before he accepted his parents’ money, Bezos made it abundantly clear to them that they might never get it back.

“I want you to know how risky this is,” Mike Bezos recalled his son saying in a 2015 interview. “Because I want to come home at dinner for Thanksgiving and I don’t want you to be mad at me.”

Bezos put the odds that his online bookseller would succeed at about 30%, which he previously said was generous given that the overall success rate for startups is closer to 10%.

A year before his parents invested, Bezos had approached 60 investors asking for $50,000 minimum investments as he sought to reach $1 million in funding. Only 22 of the people he approached agreed to invest, including his parents and two younger siblings, Mark and Christina Bezos Poore.

Still, in the end, his parents made the investment despite the long odds—and despite his stepfather’s first question about the company being “What’s the internet,” Bezos joked.

“He wasn’t making a bet on this company or this concept,” Bezos said of his stepfather in an interview with the Academy of Achievement. “He was making a bet on his son, as was my mother.”

Almost immediately after opening Amazon’s online store in 1995, Bezos told the Academy of Achievement he was surprised to see orders coming in from all 50 states and from 45 different countries.

At that time, the company had about 10 employees. By 1997, the company had grown to more than 600. It went public that year at $18 per share, and raised $54 million. Bezos became a billionaire by 1998 thanks to his 40% stake in Amazon, and today,  he holds the title of the world’s third richest person, with a net worth of $283 billion, per the Bloomberg Billionaire Index.

As for Bezos’ parents, their initial bet on their son turned out to be one of the most successful venture investments of all time. It’s unclear how many shares Mike Bezos has in his possession after his wife died last year, but the couple donated 595,027 shares to the Bezos Family Foundation from 2001 through 2016.

If Mike Bezos still retained the rest of their original 1.4 million shares, they would be worth an estimated $51.7 billion at today’s stock price, according to Fortune’s calculations. Bezos’ siblings Mark and Christina, who each invested $10,000 in Amazon in 1996, according to the prospectus, would also each have shares worth more than $1 billion today if they had never sold any.

Amazon’s shares have skyrocketed more than 208,000% since its IPO in 1997. And just last month, the company’s shares hit their all-time-high stock price of $287 per share.

The Bezos family later turned some of the wealth they got from Amazon toward philanthropy. In 2000, Mike and Jackie founded the Bezos Family Foundation with their three children—Jeff, Mark and Christina—and their spouses. Since then, the foundation has focused largely on education and child development, funding research and programs aimed at helping young people from birth through high school.

“We were fortunate enough that we have lived overseas and we have saved a few pennies so we were able to be an angel investor,” Mike said of him and his wife’s initial Amazon investment. “The rest is history.”

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5335. Iraq is challenging OPEC+'s assessment of its oil production capacity

Baghdad disputes a consultants' study that put its maximum at under 5 million barrels a day ahead of Sunday's OPEC+ meeting

Iraq has turned down OPEC+'s commissioned review of how much oil it can produce, according to Bloomberg. The dispute could spark a confrontation at the group's online meeting on Sunday, Nov 29., where OPEC and its allies, under Saudi leadership, plan to rely on the findings to set production targets.

Baghdad is contesting a study by outside consultants, who put its maximum capacity at less than 5 million barrels a day, according to Bloomberg. Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair has written to OPEC to insist that Iraq can reach 5.2 million barrels a day.

Under the review, a country given a bigger capacity figure has a firmer basis for seeking a larger output allowance, according to Bloomberg. Iraq's oil ministry and OPEC's secretariat in Vienna had not responded to requests for comment from Bloomberg as of its publication.

This year, Iraq warned it could exit OPEC unless the assessment credited it with a sufficiently large number, according to Bloomberg. Iraq later withdrew the warning. The warning came weeks after the United Arab Emirates' exit from the group, and the UAE has since pushed its production to record levels.

Iraq has bristled at OPEC+ quotas for 10 years, wanting to boost its earnings and restore an economy hurt by war and sanctions, according to Bloomberg.

The two sides have also differed on how much Iraq is producing. Iraq told OPEC its October output came to nearly 4.9 million barrels daily, the highest of the wartime period and far over its quota, according to Bloomberg. Figures that OPEC draws from outside sources put the number at 4.491 million barrels a day.

OPEC and its allies have been examining the volumes each member can technically produce as groundwork for 2027 output targets.

Separately, the International Energy Agency put Iraq's sustainable capacity at 4.87 million barrels a day in its monthly oil market report this month. The agency estimated Iraq's October output at 4.6 million barrels a day, the highest since September 2019.

#5334. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5333. Billionaire Fanatics CEO made millions as a teenager but nearly lost it all by 16: ‘Each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success’

Fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes. But the company has grown into a powerhouse in its own right, striking partnerships with nearly every major U.S. sports league, including the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and generating roughly $14 billion in annual revenue.

For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.

Rubin caught the entrepreneurial bug at just 12 years old, when most kids are more concerned with middle school homework than starting a business. By 13, he was selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania, and a year later, he had opened his own storefront just down the road from his home. He was making money quickly—and even joined up with a friend to buy a Porsche before he could legally drive.

But around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, so his customers weren’t coming.

“It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled in a recent conversation with podcaster David Senra. “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”

To get himself out of the hole, he negotiated his debts down to $35,000, went door to door borrowing money from neighbors, and used the proceeds from a new venture in the closeout business to repay his loan within three weeks. Five years later, at 21, Rubin was generating $150 million in sales, buying and selling closeout merchandise.

“I went from death in its eyes, bankrupt; thought I was a complete failure, giving up on entrepreneurship—to five years later, doing $150 million, making $10 million to $15 million a year as a kid,” Rubin said. “And so to me, each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success.”

Rubin spent just one semester at Villanova University before dropping out to focus on business. He continued building his sports merchandise operation, KPR Sports, which eventually became part of Global Sports Inc., later renamed GSI Commerce.

As the internet took off, Rubin shifted the business toward e-commerce, helping major retailers and sports teams sell merchandise online.

But the 2008 financial crisis nearly wiped him out again. Rubin had borrowed heavily against his GSI stock, which lost roughly 90% of its value during the bear market. He began calling a friend who managed a hedge fund, where Rubin had invested $5 million, repeatedly asking for his money back. After roughly 100 calls, he finally got it—with just hours to spare before the bank could seize his shares.

The business eventually rebounded and was bought by eBay in 2011 for $2.4 billion. As part of the deal, Rubin bought back the company’s sports e-commerce business, laying the foundation for today’s Fanatics.

The company has since grown into a giant valued at $31 billion in 2022, while Rubin’s personal fortune has grown to an estimated $11.6 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Still, Rubin said he wouldn’t trade the ups and downs that got him to his level of success today.

“I liked the adrenaline of fighting for my life,” Rubin said.

“If it’s the same s–t every day, it’s boring,” he added. “Business is a roller coaster. Business is an adventure. If you’re a real entrepreneur, you like that. You thrive on that.”

Fortune reached out to Fanatics for further comment.

Rubin isn’t the only successful business leader to have nearly lost it all at a young age.

In the early days of Ray Dalio building out his now-multibillion-dollar hedge fund business, he was broke, living in New York City—and had to ask his father to borrow $4,000 to help cover bills.

The experience gave him humility, but also made him develop a deep respect for those who do fail—and embrace the lessons learned.

“Anyone you see succeeding is only succeeding at the things you’re paying attention to—I guarantee they are also failing at lots of other things,” Dalio wrote.

“The people I respect most are those who fail well. I respect them even more than those who succeed. That is because failing is a painful experience, while succeeding is a joyous one, so it requires much more character to fail, change, and then succeed than to just succeed.”

Mark Cuban has echoed that failure is an inevitable part of building a successful career. On his path to a $9.8 billion net worth, he made countless early missteps—from trying to sell powdered milk to getting fired from jobs to making bad investments. The ability to not let these missteps define your entire career is what matters.

“No one is going to know or care about your failures, and neither should you,”  he said. “All you have to do is learn from them.”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5332. AEREDIUM bets parallel execution can raise blockchain speed limits

Most blockchains process transactions one at a time. AEREDIUM is testing whether running engines in parallel across regions can lift that limit.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

Blockchain developers have long struggled to process high transaction volumes without slowing down network agreement. As digital payment systems expand, developers are exploring parallel processing to increase capacity across separate locations. According to researchers at the Bank for International Settlements, the trade-off among a blockchain's transaction capacity, the concentration of its stakeholders, and its security is known as Buterin's scalability trilemma. Because traditional blockchains process transactions sequentially, high demand often triggers severe congestion and rising user fees during peak market activity.

Increasing speed on a traditional blockchain is far harder than upgrading standard corporate servers. In conventional computing, engineers simply add faster processors inside a single data center to handle heavier workloads. Yet distributed ledgers require independent computers across distant regions to verify every transfer and agree on a single shared history.

To address these constraints, Layer 1 blockchain AEREDIUM is testing a horizontal scaling model that runs multiple execution engines simultaneously. Rather than relying on a single processing environment, the architecture distributes transaction execution across separate geographic regions. During a Nov. 22 demonstration on its public test network, AEREDIUM reported deploying two execution engines roughly 4,000 kilometers apart. According to the company, each engine handled approximately 200,000 transactions per second during the trial.

Over a 10-second window, AEREDIUM reported processing 3 million individually signed transfers from 1,200 funded accounts, averaging roughly 300,000 transactions per second. The company said each transaction entered through the network's standard interface, completed execution and finalization, and incurred the applicable network fee. At its peak single second, the network finalized 41 full blocks of 10,000 transactions each, reaching 410,000 transactions per second. “We have now demonstrated 410,000 transactions in a single second across 41 full blocks, with every block recorded and available for public inspection,” said Albert Dadon, founder and CEO of AEREDIUM.

Instead of traditional energy-intensive mining or token-staking consensus, AEREDIUM uses an approach it calls Proof of Attestation. Under this design, attested software validates transactions inside isolated hardware enclaves to achieve single-block finality without waiting for multiple confirmation blocks. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, a trusted execution environment is “an area or enclave protected by a system processor.” AEREDIUM states that combining hardware-backed verification with parallel engines allows capacity to grow as new engines are added.

Still, controlled benchmarks do not automatically guarantee identical performance under continuous commercial traffic. Peak bursts of 410,000 transactions per second demonstrate short-term capacity rather than sustained output over months of complex smart-contract activity. Relying on hardware-enforced enclaves also introduces specific dependencies on processor integrity, firmware security, and reliable attestation mechanisms. Independent evaluations of larger, multi-region deployments will be necessary to confirm how well coordination holds up under heavy congestion or unexpected network outages.

Looking ahead, high-throughput parallel architectures could eventually support institutional settlement, cross-border payments, and automated trading platforms. In a June 2026 economic report, the Bank for International Settlements warned that as blockchain networks proliferate, “the benefits of scalability and efficiency are often undermined by the absence of cohesion among these frameworks.” For AEREDIUM, the long-term objective is expanding network capacity incrementally by adding regional execution engines rather than capping throughput at a fixed limit.

Ultimately, the broader significance of horizontal blockchain execution lies in shifting how developers think about network limits. Rather than treating transaction speed as a rigid ceiling, distributed execution explores whether capacity can expand alongside infrastructure demand. “Our architecture is designed to increase capacity as more execution engines are added, rather than operate toward a fixed transaction ceiling,” Dadon said. Whether parallel execution can preserve security and decentralization at global scale remains the defining test for next-generation financial networks.

#5331. Nvidia degrades U.S. national security as Chinese military snags its chips

When Super Micro compliance auditors visited a Southeast Asian customer in August 2025 to inspect thousands of servers packed with Nvidia chips, the warehouse floor looked in order. According to federal prosecutors, the scene was pure theater. The servers on hand were nonworking dummies staged for the audit; the real ones had already gone to China. When Commerce Department inspectors came later, conspirators set up the same fakes again, using a hair dryer to swap labels and serial stickers. Prosecutors say at least $510 million in servers went to China over a few weeks in spring 2025 alone.

Fifteen months later, the country is once again being asked to take tidy paperwork at face value. In less than two weeks, Nvidia’s leadership turmoil swung through an astonishing reversal. Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on November 12, and five days later the company’s chairman declared that the board “does not intend to reinstate” him. Come Monday, directors brought him back anyway, citing assurances from senior U.S. officials and concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.” President Donald Trump claimed credit for talking them into it, telling CNBC, “It’s a threat to lose him.”

Official endorsements cannot wish away the serious security record piling up in the public view. Set aside, for a moment, the scrutiny swirling around Megaspeed, the firm tied to Huang’s paramour Alice Huang, as well as the question of whether she acted as a spy. Even apart from that controversy, a largely overlooked trove of documentation proves beyond dispute that restricted and banned Nvidia chips have been illegally shipped into China, where the Chinese military has openly recorded buying elite processors to bolster capabilities aimed against the United States.

Congressional investigators, state attorneys general, and the broader national security community will inevitably unravel what transpired with Megaspeed and Alice Huang. As they pursue that thread, however, they cannot lose sight of the larger pipeline operating right under Washington’s nose. Smuggled American chips are already strengthening the Chinese Communist Party’s military power and domestic repression, fueling weapons research, design, and manufacturing alongside electronic warfare and intelligence collection. Before anyone treats Huang’s return as case closed, investigators must confront the pressing, unanswered questions still hanging over Nvidia.

Consider some of the military-linked recipients already plainly visible in public records. A Reuters investigation published November 11 found that Northwestern Polytechnical University, a military-linked institution on the U.S. export blacklist since 2001 over alleged missile proliferation, recorded an October purchase of two H200 chips through a Chinese supplier. Its cybersecurity school also contracted in January for access to two servers containing eight H200s apiece.

Some advocates point out that the H200 is an older and less sensitive chip, but the administration’s January H200 licensing relaxation explicitly did not erase restrictions on blacklisted entities. Indeed, its safeguards expressly excluded military and military-intelligence users and prohibited remote access for specified restricted parties. The university’s disturbing procurement records therefore demand a detailed explanation: what authorization, if any, covered these supplies, and which intermediary checked the actual beneficiary? Did the U.S. government authorize these sales (it would be ludicrously stupid if so), or did Nvidia fail in its responsibility to monitor its own supply chain and maintain awareness of end customers?

The Harbin Institute of Technology offers another disturbing example. When Commerce blacklisted it in 2020, the department specifically cited efforts to acquire American technology for Chinese missile programs. Yet Reuters reported this March that Harbin’s July 2025 procurement notice described a Super Micro system containing eight Nvidia A100s. Beihang University, another blacklisted institution with military ties, recorded purchasing a workstation with four A100s in March 2026.

At a minimum, all of this points to persistent demand from the Chinese military and institutions linked to it — the very institutions the controls were designed to exclude and the very institutions that want to hurt U.S. national security the most. Who is dropping the ball here?

If the Chinese military has its way, more banned Nvidia chips will soon be on their way. WireScreen reviewed more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records. The units seeking Nvidia hardware include the Rocket Force, which operates China’s land-based nuclear missiles, the Cyberspace Force, and the equipment arm of the Communist Party’s Central Military Commission. One Cyberspace Force tender for A100-class servers named a password-cracking tool as the workload. Georgetown researchers found a PLA lab requesting 16 H100s and another unit seeking a DeepSeek-linked cyber range for “intelligent attack.”  That should scare any and every American.

It is not just the Chinese military obtaining older, still-restricted Nvidia chips. There is also ample evidence that the most cutting-edge, most sensitive chips—such as the Blackwell chip, which is entirely banned from being sold into China—are still making their way into China anyway, and worse, directly into the hands of the CCP. Last month, the AI security firm Lava reported finding 32 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs operating on Chinese networks—specifically linked to state-owned China Telecom—during a study of more than 12,000 GPUs, despite a ban on Blackwell chips going to China. That comes on top of the fact that even a senior administration official says DeepSeek trained a model on banned Blackwell chips, likely in Inner Mongolia. Congressional investigators should demand answers about how these Blackwell chips are getting into China and whether Nvidia is asleep at the switch on the most basic KYC duties—know your customer.

Nvidia surely must know about the transshipment of its sensitive chips into China – as has already been proven in the public record, with a long trail of criminal indictments. Alan Hao Hsu and his company, Hao Global, pleaded guilty in October 2025. According to the Justice Department, the scheme involved at least $160 million in exported and attempted exports of restricted Nvidia H100 and H200 processors. Shipping documents concealed the goods and recipients; more than $50 million in funding originated in China. The company’s plea agreement identifies transshipment through Singapore and Malaysia. This is admitted criminal conduct involving falsified documentation and illegal exports through transshipments, yet what did Nvidia do about the facilitators of that transshipment who were still getting chips from Nvidia?

Similarly, in March, federal prosecutors alleged that defendants connected to Super Micro arranged purchases through a Southeast Asian intermediary and diverted at least $510 million in servers to China within weeks in spring 2025, then used the dummy servers described at the outset to cover their tracks. In October, broker Ting-Wei Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including export-control conspiracy and obstruction. Similarly, Taiwan has indicted a senior Nvidia manager as the central figure in faking a compliance audit so that 74 servers of top-line B300 chips could reach China. Given these apparent leaks and holes across Nvidia’s supply chain, any reasonable observer would conclude the company needs to monitor its own customers and employees far more carefully.

Whenever Washington weighs a firmer line on chips, the same warning reliably surfaces. Push Beijing too hard, skeptics caution, and China will choke off the rare earth magnets powering everything from fighter jets to electric motors. That anxiety is already dictating policy. After the administration let Nvidia resume H20 sales to China last year, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was candid about the bargain, explaining, “We put that in the trade deal with the magnets.” Export controls once considered untouchable have stayed on the bargaining table ever since.

Beijing’s current leverage is undeniable. According to the International Energy Agency, China mines roughly 60% of the world’s magnet rare earths, refines around 90%, and makes nearly 95% of finished permanent magnets. Its grip tightens further on heavy rare earths like dysprosium and terbium, which keep magnets working at high temperatures inside military hardware and electric vehicle motors. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence found that as recently as 2024, the West depended on China for 99% of those heavy minerals. Nor has Beijing hesitated to flex that advantage. Export controls imposed in April 2025 on seven heavy rare earths remain in force. In June, China blacklisted two American firms championed by federal policymakers, MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, and this month it extended a pause on broader restrictions by just two months.

Their dominance, however, is a product of policy rather than geology, and it can erode far faster than conventional wisdom expects. Rare earths are not actually rare. All 17 occur outside China, and the U.S. Geological Survey estimates that more than 40 percent of reported global reserves—and an even larger share of identified deposits—lie beyond China’s borders, including 11 million metric tons in Brazil alone, along with major deposits across Australia, Canada, Greenland, Tanzania, and the United States. As late as the 1980s, the world’s leading producer was not in Asia at all, but a single mine in California’s Mojave Desert called Mountain Pass. China assembled its commanding lead in roughly twenty years.

Japan has already demonstrated how swiftly the balance can shift. After Beijing halted exports to Japan in 2010, Tokyo bankrolled Australia’s Lynas and cut China’s share of Japanese rare earth imports from over 90% to roughly 60% within a decade. Lynas has since become the first producer outside China capable of separating both dysprosium and terbium.

The true bottleneck is not ore, but processing capacity and permits, both of which can be solved in years instead of decades. While the IEA estimates that meeting demand for magnet rare earths outside China will require roughly $60 billion over the next ten years, the figure is a modest fraction of the $1.2 trillion in U.S. economic activity Bloomberg calculates depends on these materials. Washington has begun laying the groundwork, pairing a Pentagon stake and price floor for MP Materials with the $12 billion Project Vault stockpile and $565 million for Brazil’s Serra Verde, which supplies those same vital heavy rare earths.

Permitting remains the stubborn obstacle. S&P Global calculates that taking a new American mine from discovery to production averages 29 years, slower than every country on earth except Zambia and almost ten years behind Australia. Delays on such a scale turn responsible oversight into outright paralysis. Clearing the logjam demands an “Operation Warp Speed” for critical minerals, built on hard permitting deadlines, one lead agency per project, guaranteed offtake for allied producers stretching from Brazil and Canada to Africa, and strict environmental standards enforced upfront without endless litigation. Smart environmental policy is essential, yet reflexive obstruction simply ships both the mining and the pollution straight to China.

Beijing’s rare earth card is a wasting asset, provided Washington chooses to make it one. The answer is to build, not to bend, and certainly not to keep weakening the export controls standing between America’s best technology and the People’s Liberation Army.

Congress holds subpoena power, and they ought to wield it to get to the bottom of how the Chinese military is obtaining banned Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s shipment ledger for every GPU sent to Southeast Asia since October 2022 is fair game and in the company’s possession, as are any location data its fleet-management software has collected, its customer files and communication with US regulators, including the Department of Commerce.

State attorneys general are paving the way, as California Attorney General Rob Bonta has already subpoenaed Nvidia on how chips reached China and whether investors were misled.

Export controls were meant to keep America’s best chips out of China’s war machine, yet the evidence shows that Nvidia’s most sensitive chips are already fueling the Chinese military in its quest to degrade US national security. The only crime greater than smuggling these chips into the hands of the Chinese military would be our neglect in letting them get away with it.

As the line often attributed to Lenin goes, “Capitalists will sell you the rope used to hang them.”

#5330. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5329. John Deere acquires Orchard Robotics, an AI farming startup with Seattle ties

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

#5328. Thanksgiving closure and Black Friday early close: 2026 stock market hours

Stock market hours for Thanksgiving 2026 include a full closure and a Black Friday early close, plus Christmas dates, regular Nasdaq hours and extended sessions

Thanksgiving week 2026 squeezes the U.S. stock trading calendar into a shorter stretch than usual. Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 holiday schedule lists the market as closed on Thursday, November 26. It then shows an early close at 1:00 p.m. on Friday, November 27, the day widely known as Black Friday. Anyone checking stock market hours for Thanksgiving 2026 needs both dates in view.

A normal session on the Nasdaq Stock Market runs Monday through Friday, from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. A full closure removes that session entirely. An early close trims the day, and the schedule lists 1:00 p.m. as the cutoff on the affected dates.

Those changes matter for anyone who places orders, sets price alerts or plans trades around the closing bell. An order meant for the last hour of a normal day may need different timing on a shortened one. Alerts and standing instructions tied to a 4:00 p.m. finish may need adjusting too.

December brings a second set of changes. Nasdaq's schedule lists another 1:00 p.m. early close on Thursday, December 24, followed by a full closure on Friday, December 25. Christmas Day is the final entry in Nasdaq's 2026 table. Earlier in the year, the same schedule lists Labor Day, September 7, 2026, as a closure. It is the last holiday on that list before Thanksgiving.

Holiday dates are only part of the picture. Nasdaq also publishes hours for pre-market and after-hours sessions, and some of its options venues trade until 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time. Extended-hours trading comes with thinner participation and bigger price swings, and access varies by broker.

This guide covers a selection of dates and hours from Nasdaq's published schedule, not every entry in it. The slides that follow explain the Thanksgiving closure, the shortened Black Friday session, the Christmas Eve and Christmas Day changes, the regular trading day and the extended sessions. Nasdaq offers downloadable trading calendars for 2026 and 2027, along with links to its Nordic and Nasdaq Canada schedules.

The U.S. stock market is closed all day on Thursday, November 26, 2026, for Thanksgiving. Nasdaq $NDAQ lists the date as a full closure on its 2026 U.S. stock market holiday schedule. No regular trading session runs that day.

A full closure is different from a shortened day. No session is scheduled to open, and none is scheduled to close. The date drops out of the trading calendar entirely.

Timing matters for anyone who planned to act on Thursday. An order intended for the holiday has to be placed during an earlier session or held until trading resumes. Investors who rebalance on a fixed schedule or track a position into the close can account for the missing day ahead of time.

The holiday extends beyond stock exchanges. The Federal Reserve System includes Thanksgiving Day on its list of observed holidays.

On Nasdaq's 2026 calendar, the closure listed immediately before Thanksgiving is Labor Day, Monday, September 7, 2026. No other holiday sits between those two dates on the schedule.

Investors who want the dates saved can download Nasdaq's 2026 trading calendar from the same schedule page. The 2026 schedule on that page covers U.S. markets. Nasdaq links separately to holiday schedules for its Nordic markets and for Nasdaq Canada.

Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 holiday schedule lists Friday, November 27, 2026, as an early close, with trading ending at 1:00 p.m. The market opens that day, but the session is shorter than a normal one.

That Friday follows Thanksgiving Day, Thursday, November 26, 2026, when the market stays closed. Investors returning from the holiday get one abbreviated session before the weekend.

The early close changes the trading window, not the trading date. November 27 still counts as a market day. Anyone who usually acts late in the session has less time to do it.

The schedule's entry for November 27 gives the 1:00 p.m. time without naming a time zone. Readers should confirm with their broker which time zone applies and what the local equivalent is, rather than assume it.

Anyone planning to place, change or cancel orders that Friday should ask their broker how it handles the shortened day. That check can cover whether pre-market or after-hours trading is offered on November 27. It can also cover when Nasdaq's options venues stop trading that day.

The stock market closes early at 1:00 p.m. on Thursday, December 24, 2026, and stays shut all day on Friday, December 25, 2026, for Christmas Day. Both dates appear on Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 U.S. stock market holiday schedule.

Christmas Eve brings a shortened session rather than a day off. Trading opens as usual, then stops at the 1:00 p.m. cutoff listed for that date. The cutoff removes the late afternoon that a normal weekday session would include.

The schedule leaves some questions about December 24 open. It does not say whether pre-market and after-hours sessions run that day. It also does not give closing times for Nasdaq's options venues on early-close dates. Anyone planning trades in those sessions should check how their broker handles the day.

Christmas Day is a full closure, with no regular trading session at all. In 2026, December 26 and 27 fall on a Saturday and a Sunday. The Nasdaq Stock Market's regular hours run Monday through Friday only. That leaves three consecutive days without a regular session, from Friday through Sunday. Monday, December 28, does not appear on the holiday table.

Christmas Day also matters for some investment funds whose business days follow the market calendar. One fund's supplement describes its business days as those when both the New York Stock Exchange and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York are open. The same filing lists Christmas Day among the holidays when the fund is closed. The filing also treats weekends as non-operating days for both institutions.

Christmas Day is the last entry in Nasdaq's 2026 holiday table. Investors planning further ahead can download a 2027 trading calendar from the same page.

The Nasdaq $NDAQ Stock Market trades Monday through Friday from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Six Nasdaq options venues keep trading until 4:15 p.m. ET, later than the stock market's closing bell.

That regular stock session lasts six and a half hours each weekday. It is the baseline for every date on Nasdaq's 2026 holiday schedule. The Thanksgiving, Black Friday, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day changes all alter this window.

The six options venues with the later close are Nasdaq PHLX, The Nasdaq Options Market (NOM), Nasdaq ISE, Nasdaq GEMX, Nasdaq Texas Options and Nasdaq MRX. Each one trades from 9:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. ET on a regular day. Options trading on these markets continues for a quarter of an hour after the main stock session ends.

Two other Nasdaq equities venues follow the same clock as the main market. Nasdaq Texas (NTX) equities and Nasdaq PSX both trade from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET. Their sessions open and close alongside the Nasdaq Stock Market, without the extra time the options venues get.

Trading hours are not the same as system hours. Nasdaq lists a separate system window for each venue. Those windows are wider than the regular trading session, and they differ from one venue to the next.

The Nasdaq Stock Market system runs from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET, a span of 16 hours. Nasdaq Texas (NTX) runs from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. ET, a 12-hour window. Nasdaq PSX runs from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET, or nine hours. Nasdaq PHLX and the options markets run from 7:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. ET, a span of nine hours and 45 minutes.

Every one of those system windows opens before 9:30 a.m. ET and closes after 4:00 p.m. ET. Investors who need to know exactly when an order can execute on a given venue, including during shortened holiday sessions, can confirm the details with their broker.

Nasdaq $NDAQ's pre-market session runs from 4:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. ET, and its after-hours session runs from 4:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. Both windows fall outside the regular weekday session.

The sessions connect directly to the regular day. Pre-market trading ends at 9:30 a.m. ET, the moment the regular session opens. After-hours trading begins at 4:00 p.m. ET, the moment it closes.

Together, the two windows add nine and a half hours to a normal weekday. The pre-market stretch lasts five and a half hours. The after-hours stretch lasts four. The regular session between them runs six and a half hours.

Those times describe Nasdaq's own sessions, not what every investor can reach. Nasdaq notes that some brokers set different hours for extended trading. It also notes that not every online broker offers extended-hours trading at all. Anyone who wants to place orders before the opening bell or after the close should confirm both points with their brokerage first.

Trading conditions also differ outside regular hours. Nasdaq warns that extended sessions carry lower liquidity, which means fewer participants are buying and selling. It also warns of higher volatility, with prices liable to swing more widely than during the regular day.

Holiday weeks add another variable. Nasdaq's 2026 schedule lists Thanksgiving Day, November 26, and Christmas Day, December 25, as full closures, with no regular session on either date. It lists Friday, November 27, and Thursday, December 24, as early closes at 1:00 p.m.

The schedule does not say whether pre-market or after-hours trading takes place on those two shortened days, or at what times. Investors who plan to trade outside regular hours on November 27 or December 24 should ask their broker how those sessions will be handled.
