#5317. Florida State fired Mike Norvell despite a $58.7 million buyout

Ten college football coaches carry buyouts between $49.5 million and $105.1 million. See what each price says about the school.

At the top of college football, firing a head coach has become one of the most expensive decisions a university can make. Schools have shown they will pay sums in the tens of millions of dollars to change direction. The Associated Press reports that Texas A&M owed Jimbo Fisher more than $75 million when it decided to start over. LSU also accepted a large buyout to part ways with Brian Kelly, according to CBS Sports. Both schools chose to pay that price rather than keep a coach they no longer wanted. A buyout's size alone doesn't decide whether a coach keeps his job. It sets the price a school must accept to make a change, and the wealthiest programs in the sport have shown they will accept it.

The figure attached to a coach is less settled than it looks, because it marks the most a school might owe rather than what the school ends up paying. The Associated Press reports that the amount depends largely on how many years remain on a contract. A school that waits a season before acting owes less than one that acts today. A school can also bargain. Penn State owed James Franklin $49 million when it let him go, CBS Sports reports, and the two sides settled on $9 million. That changes how to read any coach's price tag. Each figure describes a contract on one date. It says as much about what a school was willing to promise as about how secure the coach really is.

Sports Illustrated set out to identify which college football coaches would cost the most to fire, at programs ranging from Indiana and Illinois to Georgia and Florida State. Each figure is the price a school would pay to change course, not a measure of a coach's salary or skill. Some of these contracts were written to keep a winning coach in place. For those schools, a large number is a statement of how much they want to keep the man they have. Other contracts are being tested by losing seasons, and for those schools the figure is the real cost of a change they may be weighing. At least one school on the list has already made that change anyway.

Georgia has made the largest commitment to its coach of any school in college football. As of Dec. 1, 2025, firing Kirby Smart would have cost the school $105.1 million, far more than any other known buyout in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. Georgia faces a bill that large because of a promise it made, not because of a penalty clause. Bleacher Report reports that the school fully guaranteed Smart's deal if it fires him without cause through Dec. 31, 2028, and that the guarantee drops to 85% after that. Georgia's full promise therefore covers the next few seasons, and for those seasons the school has chosen to face the sport's highest price if it ever wants a change.

The contract binds Georgia far more than it binds Smart. Smart could walk away for a small part of what Georgia would owe to push him out, paying $5 million through the end of 2026, according to Bleacher Report. Smart, not the school, holds the easy way out. If another job ever tempts him, the decision is his.

Georgia has little reason to want a change, because Smart keeps winning. Under Smart, Georgia claimed back-to-back national titles in the 2021 and 2022 seasons and holds a 46-3 record over that stretch, according to Bleacher Report. That kind of winning makes the guarantee easy for the school to stand behind. Georgia wrote the largest buyout in college football to protect a coach who almost never loses. At a school with a struggling coach, a buyout is a price to weigh. At Georgia, it is mostly a statement of intent.

Georgia has promised more than any other school to keep its coach, and Smart is the one who decides whether the deal holds.

Ohio State has made one of the largest promises any school has made to keep its coach. The school would owe Ryan Day $70.9 million if it fired him, the second-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated, and his salary ranks among the top 10 in the sport. Ohio State made that commitment to a coach who had already delivered. Day won the national title in 2024, according to CBS Sports. With a promise that large, Ohio State was declaring that Day was the coach it meant to keep, more than it was buying him insurance.

A disappointing season has turned that promise into a cost Ohio State has to weigh. The Buckeyes lost four games in 2026, according to CBS Sports, a heavy total for a team that had won it all two seasons earlier. The cost of acting has also fallen since the $70.9 million figure was dated Dec. 1, 2025. A firing once the 2026 season ends would leave Ohio State with a $57.5 million bill, a figure dated Nov. 21, 2026. The drop comes from how the contract is built. Day's buyout is set as a fixed sum for each remaining year rather than a share of his remaining salary, so the total shrinks as each season passes. The longer the school waits, the less it would pay to make a change, and the less protection Day gets from his contract.

A smaller bill alone may not settle Day's future. A school should fire a coach only when it has a clearly better replacement in mind, and the market for coaches is thin right now. Day has gone 89-16 at Ohio State, according to CBS Sports, and has won the large majority of his games. For a change to pay off, Ohio State would need to find a coach who could top that record.

For Ohio State, the money is only one reason to keep Day, alongside his winning record and a short list of better options.

Alabama would pay one of the steepest prices in college football to fire Kalen DeBoer, but most of that price comes from a promise the school made before its latest move. Firing him would cost Alabama $60.8 million, the third-largest buyout among football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated. FanSided reports that DeBoer's original contract already ran through 2031, and that Alabama restructured it and added a raise rather than writing a wholly new commitment. Alabama had largely accepted its side of the bill before the new terms. The school's recent changes were aimed at the other side of the contract.

The restructuring set what DeBoer would owe if he chose to leave. Under the original deal, he could have walked away owing Alabama nothing after Jan. 31, 2027, according to FanSided. Michigan and Penn State were rumored to be interested in him, which made a free exit a real risk for the school. The new deal has DeBoer owing $10 million to leave through Jan. 31, 2027, and that gives Alabama some protection. Even so, the contract binds the school far more than the coach. In exchange for a raise, Alabama made DeBoer harder to lure away.

Alabama made this commitment before DeBoer's results could show whether he is the coach for the long run. He has gone 20-8 in his two seasons at Alabama, according to FanSided, and that record has not settled the question. The cost of firing him comes from the terms Alabama wrote, not from how often his teams win. Alabama is paying to avoid starting over, with the expense and risk of a new coaching search at a program that has to keep winning now.

At Alabama, the big number is less armor for DeBoer than a premium the school accepted to keep the coach it knows.

Texas would face such a large bill to change coaches because the school made its biggest promise to Sarkisian only recently. Firing him would cost Texas $60.3 million, the fourth-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated. Longhorns Wire reports that Texas signed the deal in 2025 and committed to Sarkisian through 2031. Nearly all of that long promise has yet to be paid. The size of the figure shows how strongly Texas bet on its coach a short time ago, more than how secure his job is today.

Texas is facing a test of that bet much sooner than the school planned when it signed the deal. The team held the No. 1 ranking only two weeks earlier, according to Longhorns Wire, and the fall since then has been fast enough that people now discuss a firing openly. "I believe, personally, that after Texas loses its third game (Texas athletic director) Chris Del Conte has an honest conversation about the firing of Steve Sarkisian," Cole Thompson, co-host of the SEC Unfiltered Podcast, told Longhorns Wire. Texas already has a possible interim coach on staff in defensive coordinator Will Muschamp. With a replacement in the building, the size of the $60.3 million check is the main reason for Texas to hold back.

The exact cost of firing Sarkisian is not a single fixed number. The $60.3 million figure dates to Dec. 1, 2025. Longhorns Wire reports a different amount for a firing after the 2026 season, putting the bill at $50.15 million. Even the lower figure would leave Texas paying tens of millions of dollars to a coach it no longer wanted.

Texas now has to decide whether one season's fast fall justifies a check that large.

Few schools have committed to a coach as firmly, or as far into the future, as Clemson has to Dabo Swinney. Firing him would have cost $60 million as of Dec. 1, 2025, the fifth-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated, and his salary also ranks among the top 10 in the sport. Clemson pays Swinney like one of the game's elite coaches and has promised to keep doing so for years. Post and Courier reports that his contract runs until 2031, so most of that $60 million covers seasons Swinney has not yet coached. The buyout records how much faith Clemson placed in Swinney when it signed the deal. It does not guarantee his future.

Clemson is now weighing that faith against a season that has gone wrong. The team is 6-4 overall and 4-3 in the ACC heading into its game at Duke $DUK, according to Post and Courier, a middling record for a program that has grown used to contending. A school with that record has good reason to ask what a change would cost. At Clemson, the answer is one of the largest bills in college football. A sum that large can make a school hesitate, but it does not take the question off the table. Any decision about Swinney would cost Clemson tens of millions of dollars, and it would be a choice the school makes on purpose.

Clemson made its promise to Swinney before this season, and after a middling year the school now has to decide whether it still wants to keep it.

Mike Norvell's contract promised him far more protection than his paycheck would suggest. Florida State agreed to a $58.7 million buyout, the sixth-largest among football coaches, even though his salary ranked only 45th in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. The school wrote the deal to make firing him very costly, not to pay him like one of the game's top earners. A price that large is meant to make a school think hard before it acts. Florida State fired Norvell on the Sunday after a loss to Clemson, The Post and Courier reports, and the size of the bill did nothing to slow the decision. The $58.7 million figure is dated Dec. 1, 2025, and is not a confirmed payout, so what Florida State will end up paying is still unsettled.

What outweighed the price was how far the team had fallen from a recent high point. Florida State went 13-0 in 2023, according to The Post and Courier, and that unbeaten season gave fans every reason for faith. The team has gone 10-23 since then and lost far more often than it won. A record that poor over so short a stretch made keeping Norvell harder to defend than paying him to leave. Once losses pile up at that rate, a buyout stops protecting a coach and becomes a cost the school decides to absorb.

The demand for a change was public before the Clemson game began. Fans at the stadium saw a plane circle overhead towing a banner that read "Fire Mike Novell + Peter Collins," with Norvell's name misspelled. The coach on the other sideline objected to the banner. "Listen, hey, I get it, man. Everybody's got contracts and all this type of stuff, but man, that bothered me," Clemson coach Dabo Swinney said, as reported by The Post and Courier. Florida State faced that pressure in full view of its own fans and its opponent.

For any school weighing whether to fire a losing coach, Florida State shows that even a huge buyout does not stop a school from acting.

Oregon put one of the steepest prices in college football on its coach while the team was at its best. Firing Dan Lanning would have cost $56.7 million as of December 2025, the seventh-largest buyout among football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated. Most of that commitment came after Lanning was hired, because his buyout was $20 million when he first signed, according to ESPN reporter Jake Trotter's figures reported by Bleacher Report. The school promised him far more as the team kept winning, and Oregon reached the College Football Playoff semifinals last January. The $56.7 million is a record of what Oregon chose to commit to Lanning while things went right. It does not show how secure he is when they go wrong.

Oregon now has to weigh that price during a slump. The team fell to 4-3 after losing to Illinois, according to Bleacher Report, which is a sharp drop for a program that played in a playoff semifinal months earlier. Oregon outgained Illinois 426 yards to 314 in that game, and the team moved the ball well but could not turn those yards into a win. It also played without its starting quarterback, Dante Moore, who missed a third straight game with a concussion. With Moore out that long, Oregon cannot yet tell whether the coach or the missing quarterback is more to blame for the losses.

Lanning has acknowledged that his team is falling short. "I think all things are on the table for us to make sure that we're the best version of ourselves, and we're currently not that. That's very clear," Lanning said, as reported by Bleacher Report. For now, Oregon would be weighing the $56.7 million against a coach who admits the team is not playing well and a starting quarterback who has missed three straight games.

At Indiana, the cost of firing Curt Cignetti moved well ahead of what the school was paying him. Indiana agreed to a buyout of $56.7 million, the eighth-largest among college football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated, even though his salary ranked only 18th in the sport. The school promised far more to keep him than it paid him to coach. Indiana used the buyout to show how badly it wanted to hold on to Cignetti, and it made that commitment before his paycheck matched it.

The gap opened because Cignetti won so quickly that other schools had good reason to want him. The $56.7 million figure dates to Dec. 1, 2025, before his biggest season was over. Indiana went on to finish 16-0 with a national title win over Miami, according to The Gazette. Each of those wins made him more costly to lose, and Indiana gave him a raise after the buyout figure was fixed.

The salary gap that put Cignetti in this company has since closed. As of March 2026, he was one of only three active FBS coaches paid $13 million or more a year, along with Georgia's Kirby Smart and Lane Kiffin, according to The Gazette. Indiana once paid him like a mid-tier hire, and it now pays him like one of the sport's elite. The mismatch was a delay rather than a lasting feature of the deal. Indiana wrote the buyout first, and the salary followed.

The $56.7 million measures what Indiana feared losing in late 2025, and the school has paid more to keep him ever since.

Nebraska does not pay Matt Rhule like one of college football's very top coaches, but firing him would cost the school more than almost any other program would pay to replace its coach. His salary ranks only 15th in the sport, yet his $49.6 million buyout is the ninth-largest among football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated. Rhule's contract with Nebraska covered eight years and $74 million in total as of 2023, according to The Associated Press. The length of that promise, not the size of his yearly paycheck, is what places him among the most expensive coaches to fire. The price shows how long Nebraska pledged to stand by its coach more than how highly it values him in any single season.

That protection is strongest at the start of the deal and weakens every year the contract runs, whether or not Nebraska does anything. In November 2023, Rhule's buyout stood at $62 million, according to The Associated Press. As of Dec. 1, 2025, Nebraska would have owed him $49.6 million, a much smaller bill only two years later. Any decision about Rhule becomes cheaper for Nebraska the longer the school waits, so the cost of firing him holds the school back less than its size suggests.

Nebraska wrote that protection on purpose. Trev Alberts, the school's athletic director in 2023, considered long terms and buyout clauses the tools that make it harder for a school to push a coach out, according to The Associated Press. He also saw the risk that those tools create for the school itself. "On the other hand, it certainly does put universities in precarious situations if it's apparent a leadership transition is required," Alberts said.

At Nebraska, the buyout is a bet that the school will never need to break its promise to Rhule, and each year he stays, Nebraska would pay less if it lost that bet.

Illinois has made Bret Bielema one of the most expensive coaches in college football to fire, and the cost runs well ahead of where his pay ranks. His $49.5 million buyout is the 10th-largest among football coaches, while his salary ranks 19th in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. The cost is high because Illinois has committed to him for a long time, not because it pays him like a star. The News-Gazette reports that Illinois has extended Bielema's contract for a second time and that the deal now runs six years. The price of firing him reflects the school's own decision to renew its bet on Bielema more than any judgment of what other schools would pay him.

Illinois wrote this contract mainly to keep its coach from leaving. Starting July 1, 2026, the school will pay Bielema a retention incentive of $700,000 each year he stays, according to The News-Gazette. "We’ll pay a premium for that kind of certainty for our program and our student-athletes," Josh Whitman, the Illinois athletic director, said. The large firing price is the other side of that premium, because it is what Illinois would owe to give up the certainty it bought.

Bielema's terms are part of a policy that covers much of the Illinois athletic department. The News-Gazette reports that several Illinois coaches have non-compete clauses in their contracts. Whitman says the school wants steady leaders at a time when college sports treats turnover as normal. Buyouts carry weight in college football because schools replace coaches so often, and Illinois has chosen to spend money to avoid doing the same.

At Illinois, $49.5 million is less a fee for firing Bielema than a measure of how hard the school has worked to make sure it never needs to.

#5315. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5313. On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

By recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

Even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”

Seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients said a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

It seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

By then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

Against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

With fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” said Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”

That job falls to the new Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t plan on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

#5310. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#5309. He Saw a ‘Weird’ Machine on Instagram, Got on a Plane to Try It and Built a $75 Million Fitness Empire

STRONG Pilates co-founder Michael Ramsey shares the making of one of the fastest-growing fitness franchises in the world.

Most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling. Michael Ramsey bought a plane ticket to check it out in person. The former oil and gas marketer, who once ran an F45 studio in Port Melbourne, saw a post about an exercise machine called the Rowformer, and flew from Australia to Orange County to try it himself. Seven years later, STRONG Pilates has more than 130 studios across multiple countries and continents, 57,000 members and more than $75 million in net revenue over the past 12 months.

Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.

This wasn’t your original career path. How did you get involved in Pilates?I was working in oil and gas, and I was not enjoying my life too much. I wasn’t highly motivated in corporate. And on the weekends, I was actually running a nightclub with my business partner, Mark Armstrong, who I’ve been in business with for eleven years. And he tapped me on the shoulder and he said, “Hey, I found this really unique boutique concept called F45 Training.” This was about twelve years ago. And so we actually brought the first F45 studio to Melbourne, Australia, and I quit my job in corporate, and for the first time in my life, I felt free, like I was in charge of my own destiny. Not only did I have financial freedom, but I had time as well. We scaled our F45 studios to six very quickly, sold after about four or five years.

What inspired STRONG?My housemate showed me an Instagram post about this Rowformer machine that was created out of Orange County. And to me it ticked a lot of boxes — you’ve got rowing, and you’ve got the Reformer. So I jumped on a plane, took the class and it was one of the most exhilarating, endorphin-led kind of workouts I’d ever done. I’m looking around the room, and there are all these incredibly fit women in their forties and fifties that just looked incredible. And I’m like, “Wow, this, this is awesome. I need to take this back to Australia.” Mark tried it, had the same experience, and then we negotiated global rights for the machine and built a franchise model around it.

Most of us see something cool on Instagram and keep scrolling. We don’t jump on a plane. What does that say about you?Look, to be transparent, it was very opportunistic. I could see, and nothing against F45, but I couldn’t see the lifetime value of the customer increasing over time due to the impact of workouts. So I was on the hunt for something that was low impact, more longevity-focused. How do we keep our members for five, six, seven, ten years? That was a question that I had and the problem I was trying to solve.

How do you turn early adopters into paying clients and repeat customers?You need to respect your product and business enough to have people paying from the start. There’s this whole thing in the fitness industry about free trials, and do they work or do they not work? We are a premium product, and I think once the work is done and the product is ready, you need to respect yourself and your product by charging for every session.

Now, for anyone who’s starting in this space, I would say the first thing to do is just start. Just open, and then learn from your consumer and innovate like crazy. And that’s all we did. It’s a very different product today than what it was seven years ago, and in another seven years it’s gonna be probably even more different, because that’s how it works. If you don’t innovate, you will recede, and you will die.

Was there an innovation that came from customer feedback and made you think, “Oh yeah, that’s a good idea”?The big one was the TV screens. Our male audience, as soon as we put TVs in, their trial-to-member conversion went through the roof. You’ve got to imagine, seven years ago, a lot of men hadn’t even experienced Pilates before. They were terrified to jump on a reformer. So the TVs, although they’re not liked by the traditionalists, gave us a huge uptake, particularly with male consumers. It was huge for us.

Your Instagram handle is just “Strong.” How on earth did you get that?Do you remember when domain names were getting really expensive? Like imagine strong.com. It’s probably worth half a million dollars. I had some friends that were trying to open businesses and trying to get these domain names, and I thought, “Well, I’m gonna start acquiring one-word Instagram names,” because Instagram was really taking off at the time. And so I had Strong, I had Cultivate, I had Ram. So I just held onto them. And then when I went to Orange County and I did the workout, I thought, “How does this workout make me feel? Not only do I need to be physically strong, but I need to be mentally strong to get through this.” And so it just made sense to call it STRONG Pilates, and now we’re here. At one point, it was getting tagged every 30 seconds all around the world, and I would just sit there watching it.

#5308. ‘We’re begging’: DOGE slashed federal workforce to its lowest in 60 years, and the Trump administration says it still can’t recruit Gen Z workers

The Trump administration is doubling down on efforts to hire young people, but the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) campaign to cull the federal workforce may now be hampering that goal.

On Nov. 12, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor visited Texas Christian University and spoke with students. The reason? Recruiting the next generation of future government workers.

It’s a big problem: People younger than 30 make up just 7% of the civil service even though the age demographic makes up 23% of the total American workforce, according to Kupor. As of January 2026, young people made up 7.9% of federal employees, down from 8.9% in September 2024 before President Donald Trump took office, according to the Partnership for Public Service.

“I need young, smart people that are coming in, willing to serve,” Duffy said. “You can do it for a lifetime. You can make a career out of it, and that’s wonderful.

“I find it fascinating that more young people don’t want to apply,” he added. “We’re begging for people to come in.”

The administration’s recruiting push has been undercut by an overhaul of the federal workforce when Trump first took office, according to Elizabeth Linos, the Emma Bloomberg Professor of Public Policy and Management at the Harvard Kennedy School. The slashes in headcount, as well as disruptions in workflow as a result of reduced staffing, are discouraging the next generation of talent from joining the federal workforce, she argued, even if DOGE has officially been disbanded for about a year.

“The government sent a message, in particular to young people, saying these jobs are not going to be safe and they’re not going to be secure,” Linos told Fortune. “Even though there are efforts to try to bring talent into government right now, the administration is basically sending two contradictory messages about whether it wants talent in the federal government to begin with, and I think people hear that conflicting message.”

OPM launched the Early Career Talent Network in March, a recruitment push for entry-level workers to apply for finance, human resources, engineering, project management, and procurement jobs within the federal government. The initiative follows the launch of the U.S. Tech Force last December, a hiring initiative for 1,000 engineers and specialists to work with private sector tech companies on the AI buildout within the government.

The Department of Transportation similarly launched a campaign in April targeting Gen Z gamers for air traffic controller roles with recruitment videos featuring popular titles like Fortnite. The agency hired more than 2,000 air traffic controllers, breaking the record in October for most air traffic controller trainees hired in a year. The department has more than 4,000 fewer employees total than it did before Trump took office, according to OPM data.

Gen Z in particular is struggling in today’s labor market, as the unemployment rate for recent college graduates exceeds that of overall unemployment, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. With concerns over AI displacement and fewer job opportunities, young people are prioritizing stability and work-life balance, Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found.

Under Elon Musk, DOGE gutted of federal agencies and implemented a deferred resignation program that saw the largest mass resignation in American history last September. Since DOGE’s inception in January 2025, the federal government is more than 258,000 roles smaller, according to Office of Personnel Management data. Even after DOGE was officially disbanded last November, sending its agents to continue their work as employees within the administration’s separate agencies, headcount decreased an additional 42,000 in 2026. About 2.68 million people work for the federal government, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released earlier this month, a decrease of about 1,000 workers from September, and the lowest since summer of 1965.

“By realigning roles, streamlining operations, and modernizing how agencies manage talent, we are strengthening performance and accountability across government,” Kupor said in a statement to Fortune. “This effort ensures taxpayer dollars support a workforce that delivers efficient, responsive, and high-quality services.”

An aging federal workforce has been a problem for years, and is not a result of DOGE or the Trump administration. The U.S. workforce more broadly is aging due to delayed retirement and extended life expectancies, but the government in particular.

The median age of a federal worker is 47 years old, per OPM data, compared to the national average of around 42 years old.

“We’ve got close to half of our population that’s within 10 years of retirement age,” Kupor told Fortune earlier this year. “So if you just did nothing else, you’ve got this major demographic challenge of a large number of people who will likely either retire or certainly be retirement-eligible over the near term, without us actually replenishing the pipeline of early-career people coming in.”

According to Linos, DOGE exacerbated the aging of the government workforce by firing primarily probationary employees, or those who had held their positions for a year or less in most cases, many of whom were early in their careers. Court documents show DOGE fired more than 24,000 probationary workers across 18 federal agencies in the first two months of its existence.

The widespread layoffs of early career workers are in tandem with rising discontent among employees who have decided to stay within the federal workforce. The Partnership for Public Service’s Public Service Viewpoint Survey conducted in March found only 7.5% of employees believed their political leaders generated high amounts of motivation in the workforce. OPM officially ended the distribution of the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey, a satisfaction and engagement assessment for federal employees, earlier this month, marking the first time in more than 20 years it will not administer the survey. Instead, individual agencies have the option to distribute their own assessment.

Taken together, Linos explained, the cuts and low morale give young job seekers a reason to look for stable work outside the federal government.

“You could imagine a world where a committed public servant thinks about whether or not the federal government is the place where they can make the biggest impact, and might decide that it’s not anymore in the same way,” Linos said. “We’re going to have to rebuild trust in government and in the idea of being able to be a public servant in government over time, and that’s going to take at least a generation. I’m not optimistic about the short-term impacts being reversible.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5306. A Thanksgiving Feast for 10 People for Just $35? Why Grocers Are Willing to Lose Money on Your Holiday Dinner.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From Walmart to Aldi, grocers are using meal bundles to attract customers.

Popular supermarkets are using discounted Thanksgiving meal bundles to get shoppers through their doors — in the hopes that they will buy more once they are inside.

According to a new report from The New York Times, grocers are willing to lose money on holiday meal bundles because they’re betting shoppers will buy more than just the turkey. Supermarkets are sacrificing profits on Thanksgiving dinner to win more of a shopper’s overall grocery spending.

Their familiar draw is a bargain in the form of a discounted turkey or a low-priced package of Thanksgiving essentials. Such offers are called loss leaders, meaning that stores charge less than they paid suppliers in hopes of attracting shoppers who will buy other items.

For example, in October, the grocery chain Hy-Vee initially offered a bundle of 26 items that could feed 10 people for $39. The deal included a frozen turkey of up to 12 pounds, gravy mix and corn muffin mix.

A few days after offering the deal, the chain lowered the price to $35 to better match or beat offers from national grocery stores. The main competitor was Walmart, which introduced a “feast for 10” that bundles a turkey with sweet potatoes and gravy mix for $35 starting in October.

Meanwhile, Aldi’s holiday meal deal for 10 people, including a 16-pound turkey, comes out to $39, while Amazon’s grocery offer feeds six people for $25.

There is ample demand for these deals. Walmart CEO John Furner recently told Business Insider that the retailer has “sold a million more turkeys” than it did a year ago. “The customer response is strong,” he said.

Walmart store workers also mentioned to Business Insider that demand for the Thanksgiving feast is strong.

“The meal deal frenzy has been nuts!” a worker in Oklahoma said. “I work at a neighborhood market, and we are still experiencing a higher volume.”

Grocery stores are using Thanksgiving as a way to show new customers what they have on the shelves. Customers come in for the deal and leave with more than they anticipated.

“Thanksgiving is one of the biggest grocery occasions of the year, and it is our chance to show millions of shoppers what we have to offer,” Scott Patton, chief commercial officer at Aldi, said in an interview with the Times.

Other grocers are offering more expensive meal bundles. Costco’s $199 Thanksgiving spread included a five-pound precooked turkey breast, accompanied by ready-made mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, apple cobbler and pumpkin pie. Orders closed in mid-November.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles luxury grocer Erewhon is taking a pricier approach with its $749 “Ultimate Organic Feast,” which serves up to 10 people. The menu pairs a cooked free-range turkey with sourdough and roasted vegetable stuffing, rainbow carrots, garlic mashed potatoes and turkey gravy, along with a deep-dish pumpkin pie.

These prices are outside the norm. Americans will spend $58.63 on average feeding 10 people this Thanksgiving, up 6% annually, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. The increase stems from a 10% increase in turkey prices.

#5305. ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the company announced in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

The fund can grow. Anthropic says its board may add another 2% of the company for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company said it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the company matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to plan documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

That money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

The third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts, and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

The cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

Some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter, and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a company spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic says it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

The next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the company’s matches can start to move.

Until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

#5304. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5303. He Spent Two Years Teaching Strangers to Cook on YouTube Before Opening His First Restaurant. Here’s What It Did for His Business.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Watch now to learn how Jason Ganahl built a barbecue audience on YouTube, what he looks for in a hire and how he grew GQue BBQ.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

By the time Jason Ganahl opened his first barbecue restaurant, he’d already spent close to two years showing people how to cook on YouTube. He opened GQue Championship BBQ in Westminster, Colorado, in November 2015.

Ganahl was winning barbecue competitions, and friends were asking him for help with dinner. One was thinking about smoking salmon over the weekend. Others wanted to know how to grill asparagus or cook lobster tails.

He’d watched Greg Mrvich demonstrate barbecue techniques on Ballistic BBQ. Ganahl could do the same with the questions his friends were asking. Once he put an answer on YouTube, anyone who wanted to smoke salmon could find it and watch him do it.

“YouTube was born out of, I like to just share, I like to give,” Ganahl says. “That’s why the restaurant industry is great to me.”

At GQue, that means helping his team and giving the people who come in for barbecue a good experience. He describes the goal as giving guests “the best 20 minutes of their day.”

Ganahl knew his way around a smoker. Making videos gave him something to learn from scratch. He believed video would become a bigger part of how people told their stories and wanted to learn how to do the work himself.

“I thought this was a good opportunity to teach myself how to edit, create content and learn how to be pretty good at it,” he says.

“Shorts have really taken over,” Ganahl says.

He singled out Meat Church as a channel still doing long-form videos well. Asked whether he plans to make more himself, he says, “I don’t have the bandwidth to do that.”

Ganahl’s older videos are still up. Anyone looking for help with lobster tails can find his answer without ever setting foot in GQue.

Ganahl wants guests to leave GQue and tell a friend where they ate. If enough people do that, he says, the demand for another restaurant takes care of the decision about when to open one.

“Then we’re forced to grow and open up a new spot,” Ganahl says.

That’s why he pays so much attention to who he hires. He wants people who care as much as he does about what a guest gets when they walk in for lunch. When someone brings a friend back for the brisket, both should get the same barbecue that earned the recommendation.

“I’ve never been able, and I’ve never seen anybody, to be able to take chicken shit and turn it into chicken salad,” Ganahl says.

He looks for people who share his priorities and trusts them to deliver on those priorities every day. At GQue, that means smoking brisket over hickory for same-day service and keeping the price within reach for someone who wants barbecue on an ordinary day.

GQue has grown from one restaurant in Westminster to six standalone restaurants and seven concession stands across three stadiums. Two of those stands are inside Folsom Field, where GQue serves fans on game days and feeds the University of Colorado football team and staff. The company also runs two stands at Empower Field and three at Coors Field.

Ganahl started cooking barbecue at weekend competitions. Now there are people serving it on GQue’s behalf at counters across Colorado. He credits the people he’s hired with giving guests a reason to come back and bring someone else. Having a team to share the work with has also made the business more enjoyable for him.

“It’s way more fun doing it with more people than trying to do everything on your own,” he says.

#5302. Selling Your Business? Make These 3 Moves to Reduce Taxes and Protect Your Assets From Lawsuits.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The planning that actually changes the outcome of a business sale lives primarily in three strategies, and each one should be considered well in advance of marketing the company for sale.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner shows up at my office, in the middle of selling their company, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate plan is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

The planning that actually changes the outcome of an exit lives primarily in three strategies that have been authorized by the Tax Code for decades, and every one of them should be considered well in advance of marketing the company for sale.

The Tax Code imposes a federal estate tax at death equal to 40% to the extent your reported net worth — including your business, real estate and other illiquid assets — exceeds the federal estate tax exemption (currently $15 million per person for 2026).

In addition, some states impose their own inheritance tax or estate tax, which can result in a combined rate ranging from 40-75%. States oftentimes have very low and costly exemption limits, many starting at $1-2M.

The government expects a cash payment within nine months after death. Although some estates heavily concentrated in businesses or illiquid assets can qualify for installment payments, the IRS requires liens and reporting — so you are effectively putting your spouse and children in business with the IRS as their de facto partner.

The easy fix is to take action before your company jumps in value. Specifically, you should transfer all or a portion of your business shares to an irrevocable gift trust for your spouse and/or children while the company is still private and appraisable at a defensibly low discounted value (allowing you to transfer the shares within the $15 million gift tax limit).

Properly done, every dollar of appreciation on your business shares happens outside your estate. In addition, the assets inside the trust are protected from future personal lawsuits.  These benefits can continue indefinitely for the benefit of your heirs.

Most business owners balk at the word “irrevocable” when considering this planning.  However, so-called “optimized” irrevocable gift trusts can let you keep far more control than you might expect. For example, you can:

Suppose you own a company and expect to sell the company for $30 million in 18 months. Moving 40% of the shares into a trust today removes roughly $12 million from your estate, plus whatever that 40% position grows to before (and after) the sale. If the deal falls through and the business doubles to $60M in three years, you have just removed $24 million of value from the 40% estate tax ($60M x 40%).

For the seller of a company, a charitable lead annuity trust (CLAT) is the most underused financial tool that I am aware of.

With a CLAT, you transfer assets into a trust account before December 31 of the year of the sale.  The CLAT pays a fixed annual amount to the charities that you choose for a term of years (typically 20-30 years — the longer, the greater the benefits), and whatever investments remain in the CLAT account are returned to you (or your heirs).

For example, an optimized CLAT (zeroed-out grantor trust with maximum IRS-approved charitable backloading) gives you an income tax deduction in the year of the sale equal to nearly 100% of your contribution to the CLAT, and returns a significant amount back to you (assuming a reasonable 7-8% rate of return). The payments to charity are set using the IRS interest rate in effect when you fund the CLAT, and these rates are reasonably low.

Since the charitable payments are back-loaded, most of the donations from the CLAT happen in the final years … after the assets have presumably compounded to a very large amount. After all donations are made, everything left in the CLAT account passes to your heirs, without any gift tax (and without consuming any of your lifetime $15 million gift tax exemption).

Suppose you sell your company for a $20 million gain and fund a 30-year optimized CLAT with $4 million. You would receive a tax deduction equal to approximately $4 million, the CLAT would donate approximately $14 million over the 30-year period, and your children could expect to receive back approximately $10 million (assuming 7% rate of return), free of the 40% federal gift tax. The caveat, however, is that the CLAT funds cannot be spent during the 30-year term, and this strategy only makes sense if you are charitably inclined.

Section 1202 of the Tax Code lets a founder exclude up to $10 million of gain on the sale of qualified small business stock (QSBS) — and for shares issued after July 4, 2025, that figure rises to $15 million with partial benefits starting at year three instead of year five.

A married couple can multiply that exclusion by placing shares in special non-grantor trusts (each of which counts as its own taxpayer).

Here is the catch that disqualifies many of the founders that I talk to: QSBS only exists for C corporations, and the holding period starts when the C corporation issues the stock. If you have run your company as an S corporation or LLC for 15 years, you have zero qualifying years. Converting the month before the sale accomplishes nothing.

Check your state, too. For example, California does not conform to the federal QSBS exclusion, which means a founder who is a California tax resident saves federal tax only.

Every one of the moves above is irrevocable, and requires a team (including a trust attorney, CPA and appraiser) with unique technical expertise and experience.

But all three share a single feature: They only work if you plan ahead. The owner who calls the attorney after the term sheet is signed has drastically limited their options — and increased their tax bill.

If a sale is possible in the next two to three years, put an estate planning meeting on your calendar today. You spent a decade building the business. Spend one quarter planning so your business is “built to sell” in the event of an exit.

It’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner shows up at my office, in the middle of selling their company, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate plan is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

#5300. Meet the Indigenous Founder and Investor Teaching People How to Manifest Their Dream Businesses: ‘The Folks Who Are Winning Are Thinking Differently’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Betsy Fore’s entrepreneurial journey kicked off over 20 years ago.

Betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

“It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.

She launched WonderWoof, one of the first dog activity monitors, in 2014. She was the co-founder and CEO of Tiny Organics, a company delivering organic, nutrient-rich meals for babies and toddlers. Her nonprofit career accelerator, Natives Rising, empowers indigenous communities with technology, entrepreneurship and wellness.

Currently, she’s the founder and managing director of Velveteen Ventures, investing in solutions for children and the planet for the next seven generations. “Velveteen was built on my deep inner why. Before you build anything externally, you have to excavate why you’re building it at the level of your soul — not just your resume.”

What’s more, Fore just announced the launch of Velveteen Labs, a first-of-its-kind studio model that allows children to be shareholders in incubated companies. Shares are placed into a trust, and when the children turn 18, they give a majority of them to a cause of their choice.

“She’s showing that investing in Indigenous and Gen Alpha-focused founders isn’t a trade-off between impact and returns,” Roy Swan, director of mission investments at Ford Foundation and author of Positive Sum: How Zero-sum Thinking Broke Capitalism—and How We Can Fix It, says. “It’s simply good investing, done with the next seven generations in mind.”

Needless to say, Fore has accomplished a lot over the course of her career, and she’s met many entrepreneurs along the way. There’s one thing that always gets her very excited within the first five minutes of a conversation: when the person has a unique insight, based on lived experience, into the problem they set out to solve.

“You can just see when someone is speaking from their authentic self,” Fore explains. “It’s not really a sales pitch at that point. They’re literally saying, ‘I’ve tried everything. This is what worked for me. This is how I’m going to try to bring it to market.’”

Entrepreneur sat down with Fore to learn exactly how founders can reach that authentic place and accomplish the goals they set for themselves.

Fore’s book, Built on Purpose: Discover Your Deep Inner Why and Manifest the Business of Your Dreams, “breaks down how to go from idea to making something real through a values-driven approach,” Michael Acton Smith, co-founder of meditation space company Calm, shared in a statement.

Uncovering that deep inner why, and bringing the idea to life, starts with lessening the focus on external relationships — with customers, investors, and board and team members — and looking inward, Fore says.

Fore highlights the centuries-old practice of anchoring as an example of how to kick off the process. “ When yogis put their index finger and thumb together in meditation, it’s not just a pose,” she explains. “That gesture is a signal through your nervous system. It’s connecting your individual consciousness to something larger than yourself.”

Fore encourages founders to build their own version of that practice, and it begins with identifying your values. For instance, in her own life, Fore draws on the seven grandfather teachings that guide her Turtle Mountain Chippewa tribe: love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility and wisdom.

Whatever your individual values are, the next step is to physically anchor and embody those values day to day, Fore notes.

“Lean into them with a gesture, a breath, a word, so that when you walk into a fundraising meeting or have a hard call, you’re not operating from the scarcity mindset, but instead one of abundance,” Fore says. “You’re operating from who you actually are.”

Manifesting the results you want to see also plays a key role in success, Fore says.

A study conducted by Dr. Gail Matthews, a psychology professor at Dominican University of California, showed that people are 42% more likely to achieve their goals if they write them down every day.

Fore recommends opening your laptop each morning and starting with a simple sentence.

“Write it in the ‘I am’ present moment,” Fore explains. “I am building this for. I am building this because. So it’s not the pitch. It’s the real reason. The act alone changes your follow-through at a neurological level, if you’re able to live as if it’s already happening.”

Additionally, Fore says a therapeutic model called Internal Family Systems (IFS), developed by Dr. Richard Schwartz in the 1980s, can support in taking the next step toward a desired future.

The idea is that we’re not one unified self; we’re a whole system of parts, and each one has a job to do, Fore says.

“ Some of them are what IFS calls exiles, and those are the wounded or the younger versions of us that formed in hard moments in our life, the ones that carry the shame or the fear, the grief,” she explains. “Essentially, embodying that sort of scarcity mindset. And then there are the protectors, the parts that showed up to keep those exiles safe. For instance, your inner critic, that’s a protector.”

A lot of leadership advice tells people to push past fear, silence their inner critic and be more confident to get what they want. However, while Fore acknowledges there can be some value in that, she also believes that being afraid can only get you so far. Instead of simply fighting fear, she encourages founders to engage with it.

“Literally, out loud or in your head, identify it and ask what that part wants — the answer incorporates parts you love about yourself and want to bring to the forefront,” she says.

Fore points to difficult conversations with a team as an example. Instead of asking why an issue wasn’t flagged sooner, she can admit that part of her feels frustrated, then express gratitude it was caught.

“ This is a leader who’s not being hijacked by these exiles in the middle of a critical moment,” she says. “The folks who are winning are thinking differently.”

When founders do look outward and consider their relationship to customers, they might be using a transactional lens — Fore admits she made the same mistake in the beginning.

Instead, Fore suggests flipping the traditional fundraising model on its head and asking, What if the foundation of every product was built with the customer in mind, and every bit of capital was leveraged to return exponential value to them?

“ That shift from extraction to service is the difference between founders who build loyal communities and founders who churn customers,” Fore says. “So if you can ask yourself every single day, Who isn’t being served right now? That question is where your next great idea lives.”

Fore put that idea into practice when she launched Tiny Organics, which scaled to more than $13 million in sales in 24 months.

Fore sent an email to a local parent group in Park Slope, asking if other people were also interested in getting their babies to eat real fruits and vegetables that didn’t come from a pouch. She received hundreds of messages in response and had to cap the project at 100 families within two hours.

Those 100 founding families helped develop Tiny Organics’ first hero product and led to a series of supper clubs introducing kids to their first 100 flavors; those ultimately expanded to Boston, Atlanta and Chicago.

Fore’s customer-first approach that continues to resonate with the companies Velveteen Ventures invests in today.

“We wanted partners who see caring for families as one of the most important economies of our time,” Emily Greenberg, president and co-founder of AI family assistant Joy Parenting Club, says. “Velveteen leads in the care economy, and Betsy gets it in a way few investors do as a previous founder in this category. She knows that when you support parents, you’re investing in the next generation.”

These days, in the age of AI, the soft skills have become the hard skills, Fore says, noting they’re the foundation of everything she’s seen actually work in business — and she looks forward to leaning on them now and in the years to come.

“ I have so much hope,” Fore says. “You can probably tell I’m an eternal optimist. I’m going to turn everything into a victory in life. Then, inevitably it happens, where you’re able to figure it out and find a way. I know that’s been true for me, and for so many of the founders that we funded.”

Betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

“It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.
